problems.title: The balanced factor maximizes the negative lower bound
claim: Theorem 4 says the balanced S minimizes a negative descent lower bound and uses it to explain improved descent.
analysis: The positive trace sum \(g(S)=\operatorname{tr}(XS)+\operatorname{tr}(YS^{-1})\) is minimized at the balanced \(S_b\). Multiplication by \(-\eta\|G\|_2^2\) reverses the extremum: the negative bound is maximized there, not minimized. In the admissible rank-one quadratic with \(A=B=e_1\), \(\eta=0.01\), the bound is \(-0.02\) at \(s=1\) and \(-0.0425\) at \(s=4\). The exact post-step losses from \(0.5\) are \(0.480298005\) and \(0.458498880\), so balancing need not give the larger one-step decrease.
result: Theorem4 reverses the extremum of its signed descent bound. The balanced factorization does not universally give the larger exact one-step loss decrease.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.
repair: Correct the minimum to a maximum and remove or separately prove the stronger descent conclusion. The balanced-factor formula itself remains valid.
problems.impact_rationale: Theorem 4 reverses the extremum after multiplying by a negative factor, and an exact admissible update contradicts the stronger balanced-descent interpretation. This is a substantial central reasoning error.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The GD invariance theorem does not cover AdamW
problems.source_location: Theorem 6, p.7; Appendix B.6; reflora.py optimizer hooks.
claim: Theorem 6 proves a balanced gradient-descent factorization invariance.
analysis: Equivalent factors \((1,1)\) and \((2,1/2)\) give equal SGD weight change \(-0.0199\) in the scalar example, but initial AdamW normalization gives about \(-0.0199\) and \(-0.0249\) at learning rate \(0.01\). Coordinatewise adaptive normalization and optimizer state do not automatically respect the GD factor transformation. This is a scope boundary, not a counterexample to the GD theorem.
result: The invariance theorem concerns the specified gradient-descent update; current adaptive-optimizer integration does not inherit that property automatically. No contradiction to the restricted GD theorem is asserted.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.
repair: State AdamW as a separate empirical algorithm. A general adaptive-state invariance proof remains unavailable.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Different surrogate optima need a consistent branch
problems.source_location: Theorem 3, pp.4–5; linkage to Theorem 6 and default balanced rule.
claim: Theorem 3 admits multiple small-step surrogate minimizers, while Theorem 6 uses balanced factors.
analysis: For \(A=e_1,B=e_2,G=e_1e_1^\top,L=1,\eta=0.1\), the surrogate is \((s+1/s-10)^2\). Both \(s=5+\sqrt{24}\) and \(s=5-\sqrt{24}\) are global zero minima, but yield weight changes about \(-0.98989795e_1e_1^\top\) and \(-0.01010205e_1e_1^\top\). Arbitrary minimizer selection does not define a unique update. The default fixed balanced branch is not contradicted.
result: The optimizer-set statement does not select a unique update when different allowed surrogate minimizers are chosen. The default fixed balanced branch remains a countercontrol.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.
repair: Specify the balanced or equivalence-consistent branch when combining the theorems; no default-algorithm error is inferred from nonuniqueness.
